title: Without try-except: the program crashes
blurb: Entering 0 for B raises ZeroDivisionError on the division line. Nothing after it runs - not even the last print.

notes.1: int() turns the text into a number, so a = 10.
notes.2: b = 0. Zero is a perfectly valid int, so this line is fine.
notes.3: 10 // 0 is undefined, so Python raises ZeroDivisionError. There is no try-except, so nothing handles it and the program crashes here. Lines 4 and 5 never run.

title: try-except: an error jumps to except
blurb: Line 4 raises, so lines after it inside the try block are skipped; execution continues in the except block and then after the whole construct.
code: print('a // b is not possible as b is 0')

notes.1: int() turns the text into a number, so a = 10.
notes.2: b = 0. Zero is a perfectly valid int, so this line is fine.
notes.3: Entering the try block: Python now watches the lines inside it for exceptions. Nothing visible happens yet.
notes.4: 10 // 0 raises ZeroDivisionError. The rest of the try block (line 5) is skipped and Python looks for a matching except.
notes.6: A bare except matches every exception, so control jumps here.
notes.7: The except body runs: the program handles the problem and prints a friendly message instead of crashing.
notes.8: Execution continues after the whole try-except. The program ends normally - graceful termination.

title: try-except: no error means except is skipped
blurb: Same program, valid input. The try block runs to the end, the except block is skipped entirely.
code: print('a // b is not possible as b is 0')

notes.1: int() turns the text into a number, so a = 10.
notes.5: Prints the result. This is the last line of the try block.
notes.8: No exception happened, so the except block (lines 6-7) was skipped entirely. Execution continues after the construct.

title: Several except blocks: first match wins
blurb: int('abc') raises ValueError. Python checks the except clauses top to bottom and runs the first one whose class matches.
code: index = int(input('Enter Index to get value '))
print(f'in array L at {index} value is {L[index]}')

notes.4: int('abc') cannot convert the text, so Python raises ValueError. Line 5 is skipped.
notes.6: Is a ValueError an IndexError? No - skip this clause.
notes.8: Is a ValueError a TypeError? No - skip this clause.
notes.10: Is it a ValueError? Yes - this clause matches and msg now refers to the exception object.
notes.11: Prints the message stored in the exception.
notes.12: The program carries on after the try statement.

title: Several except blocks: IndexError matches first
blurb: Index 10 is valid for int() but out of range for the list, so the very first clause matches and the others are never checked.
code: index = int(input('Enter Index to get value '))
print(f'in array L at {index} value is {L[index]}')

notes.5: L[10] does not exist (valid indexes are 0 to 4), so Python raises IndexError while evaluating the f-string.
notes.6: Is it an IndexError? Yes - the first clause matches, so the TypeError and ValueError clauses are never checked.
notes.12: The program carries on after the try statement.

title: No matching except: the exception escapes
blurb: There is no ValueError clause, so the error is not handled: the program stops with a traceback and the last print never runs.
code: index = int(input('Enter Index to get value '))
print(f'in array L at {index} value is {L[index]}')

notes.6: Is a ValueError an IndexError? No.
notes.8: Is a ValueError a TypeError? No. No clauses are left, so the exception is not handled.
notes.final: No except clause matches ValueError, so the exception leaves the try statement and the program stops with a traceback. The last print never runs.

title: One except for several exception types
blurb: Put the classes in a tuple to share one handler. The exception object is bound to the name after as.
code: index = int(input('Enter Index to get value '))
print(f'in array L at {index} value is {L[index]}')

notes.6: The tuple (IndexError, TypeError, ValueError) matches if the exception is any one of them. IndexError is in the tuple, so this handler runs.
notes.8: The program carries on after the try statement.

title: try-except-else: else runs only on success
blurb: No exception was raised, so the except block is skipped and the else block confirms the try block finished cleanly.
code: index = int(input('Enter Index to get value '))
print(f'in array L at {index} value is {L[index]}')

notes.5: L[2] is 30, so this prints fine and the try block finishes with no exception.
notes.9: No exception happened, so the else block runs. It confirms the try block succeeded.

title: try-except-else: else is skipped after an error
blurb: Index 10 raises IndexError, the except block handles it, and the else block is skipped.
code: index = int(input('Enter Index to get value '))
print(f'in array L at {index} value is {L[index]}')

notes.6: except Exception matches (IndexError is a kind of Exception).
notes.7: Prints the error message. The else block (lines 8-9) is skipped because an exception happened.

title: finally runs even when an error occurred
blurb: The error is handled by except, else is skipped, and finally still runs.
code: index = int(input('Enter Index to get value '))
print(f'in array L at {index} value is {L[index]}')

notes.7: Prints the error message. The else block is skipped.
notes.11: finally runs no matter what happened above - here after the handled error.

title: finally also runs when there is no error
blurb: No error: else runs, then finally runs. finally runs in both cases, that is its job.
code: index = int(input('Enter Index to get value '))
print(f'in array L at {index} value is {L[index]}')

notes.11: finally runs here too: with or without an exception, it always runs.

title: finally inside a function with return
blurb: return c is executed first, but finally runs before the function really hands control back to the caller.

notes.1: def creates the function div. The body does not run yet.
notes.9: Calling div(10, 2). A new frame for div appears on the call stack.
notes.2: Entering the try block inside div.
notes.4: return c prepares to return 5 - but a finally block is attached, so Python runs it before leaving the function.
notes.8: finally runs even though the function was already returning. After it, the value 5 goes back to the caller.

title: finally while an exception propagates
blurb: div(10, 0) fails, the except block re-raises, finally still prints, and only then does the exception continue to the caller (and crash the program).

notes.9#1: Calling div(10, 0). A new frame for div appears on the call stack.
notes.2: Entering the try block inside div.
notes.5: The except clause matches ZeroDivisionError and binds it to err.
notes.6: raise ZeroDivisionError throws a fresh exception from inside the handler, so it will leave the function.
notes.8: finally still runs before the exception leaves the function - this is what makes it ideal for clean-up (closing files, releasing connections).
notes.final: The new ZeroDivisionError propagates to the caller at line 9. Nothing there handles it, so the program stops. print(z) never runs.

title: Nested try: the inner handler catches it
blurb: The bad second number raises ValueError inside the inner try, whose own except handles it. The outer try never sees an error.

notes.4: int('abc') raises ValueError. The inner try is the innermost one, so its handlers are checked first.
notes.7: Inner clause 1: is it a ZeroDivisionError? No.
notes.9: Inner clause 2: is it a ValueError? Yes - handled here, the outer except is never consulted.
notes.10: Prints the inner message. The program then ends normally.

title: Nested try: only the outer handler fits
blurb: The bad first number fails before the inner try is even entered, so the outer except handles it.

notes.2: int('abc') raises ValueError. The inner try has not even been entered yet, so it cannot help.

title: Nested try: ZeroDivisionError inside
blurb: Zero is a valid int, so the first int() calls pass; the division fails and the inner ZeroDivisionError handler prints the message.

notes.7: The inner except ZeroDivisionError matches and binds the exception to e.

title: Practice: nested try, inner error swallowed
blurb: The inner except handles ValueError, but index was never assigned. The next line then fails with UnboundLocalError (a kind of NameError), and the outer handler for NameError catches it.

notes.15: Calling fun_with_valueError(). A new frame appears on the call stack.
notes.4: Outer try begins inside the function.
notes.6: int('abc') raises ValueError, so index is never assigned.
notes.8: logger.exception(e) records the problem and the program carries on - but index still has no value.
notes.9: L[index] reads index, which was never assigned. Inside a function this is an UnboundLocalError (a subclass of NameError). Python says: cannot access local variable 'index'.
notes.12: Is it a NameError? Yes - UnboundLocalError is a NameError subclass, so this clause matches.
notes.13: Logs the message. The function ends normally.

title: Practice: forgetting the NameError handler
blurb: Same flow without an except NameError clause: UnboundLocalError escapes the function and the program ends with a traceback.

notes.13#1: Calling fun_without_valueError(). A new frame appears on the call stack.
notes.6: int('abc') raises ValueError, so index is never assigned.
notes.8: logs the error and continues - index still has no value.
notes.9: L[index] fails with UnboundLocalError because index was never assigned.
notes.10: Is it an IndexError? No. The outer try has no other clause, so the exception is not handled.
notes.final: UnboundLocalError escapes the function and nothing at the call site handles it, so the program stops with a traceback (exit code 1). Adding except NameError fixes it.

title: raise: the function reports a problem to its caller
blurb: fun_div raises ZeroDivisionError itself when b is 0. The exception travels up the call stack to the try block that called it.

notes.8: Entering the try block at module level.
notes.9: Calling fun_div(10, 2). A frame for fun_div appears on the call stack.
notes.2#1: b is 2, which is not 0, so the if branch runs.
notes.4: return sends 5.0 back to the caller and the frame disappears.
notes.11: Calling fun_div(10, 0). A new frame appears.
notes.2#2: b is 0, so the condition is False and the else branch runs.
notes.6: raise ZeroDivisionError creates and throws the exception on purpose. The function stops here and the exception travels to the caller.
notes.12: Back in the caller, except Exception matches.
notes.13: logger.exception(msg) prints the message. A ZeroDivisionError raised without arguments has an empty message, so an empty line is printed.

title: User-defined exception: NegativeError
blurb: area() raises the custom NegativeError for a negative dimension; the except block receives it and shows its __str__ message.

notes.1#1: Python starts creating the class NegativeError, a subclass of Exception.
notes.2: def __init__ is stored in the class (it runs later when an object is created).
notes.5: def __str__ is stored too: it controls what print(e) or logging shows.
notes.15: Calling area(-5, 10). A frame for area appears on the call stack.
notes.9: length is -5, so length > 0 is False and the else branch runs.
notes.12: raise NegativeError() creates the exception object (which runs __init__) and throws it.
notes.3: Inside __init__ the message '-ve Dimension' is stored on the exception object.
notes.16: Back in the caller, except Exception matches the NegativeError (it inherits from Exception).
notes.17: logger.exception(msg) shows the message produced by __str__: -ve Dimension.

title: User-defined exception: the minimal form (PDF)
blurb: class MyError(Exception): pass is enough. raise MyError('My Error') passes the message to the exception.

notes.1#1: Python starts creating the class MyError, a subclass of Exception.
notes.2: pass: the class adds nothing new. It still works as a custom exception type because it inherits everything from Exception.
notes.5: raise MyError('My Error') throws the exception with the message 'My Error'.
notes.6: except MyError matches exactly and binds the exception to e.
notes.7: print(e) shows the message: My Error.

title: Practice: logging an exception
blurb: The handler hands the exception to logger.exception(), which records the message (and, in real logging, the full traceback) instead of crashing the program.

notes.8: Calling fun_divide_number(10, 0). A frame appears on the call stack.
notes.6: logger.exception(msg) logs the error at ERROR level. In the real program this also prints the full traceback to the log. The function returns None.
notes.9: The program carries on and prints the last line.

title: Logical error: no exception, wrong answer
blurb: Both branches print a, so the program never reports 50 as the greater value. Nothing crashes, which is why logical errors are the hardest to find. (Also: input() returns text, so the comparison is between strings.)
code: print(f'From A and B {a} is greater value')
print(f'From A and B {a} is greater value') # Logical Error

notes.1: input() always returns text: a = '10' (a string, not a number).
notes.4: '10' > '50' compares the strings character by character: '1' is smaller than '5', so the condition is False and the else branch runs.
notes.7: This is the logical error: the else branch prints a, not b. The program runs without any exception but reports the wrong answer.

title: Runtime error: TypeError from input()
blurb: Both values are strings, and // is not defined for strings, so Python raises TypeError at runtime.

notes.4: // is not defined for two strings, so Python raises TypeError. int(input(...)) would have avoided it.
